title: Experimental Methods to Study Human Postural Control
protocol: Prepare a definite outline of all trials to be performed.
Make a checklist for data collection.
Provide the subject with a consent form containing all necessary information.
Ask the subject to read the consent form thoroughly.
Answer any questions from the subject regarding the consent form.
Have the subject sign the consent form.
Record the subject’s weight, height, and age.
Use single differential electrodes with an inter-electrode distance of 1 cm for EMG measurement of ankle muscles.
Use an amplifier with an overall gain of 1000 and a bandwidth of 20−2000 Hz.
Locate and mark the electrode attachment areas according to Seniam project guidelines.
Attach electrodes to the medial gastrocnemius at the most prominent bulge of the muscle.
Attach electrodes to the lateral gastrocnemius at one-third of the line between the head of the fibula and the heel.
Attach electrodes to the soleus at two-thirds of the line between the medial condyles of the femur and the medial malleolus.
Attach electrodes to the tibialis anterior at one-third of the line between the tip of the fibula and the tip of the medial malleolus.
Shave the marked areas with a razor.
Clean the skin with alcohol.
Allow the skin to dry thoroughly.
Shave a bony area on the patella for the reference electrode.
Clean the shaved area of the patella with alcohol.
Have the subject lie in a relaxed supine position.
Place the reference electrode on the cleaned area of the patella.
Attach the electrodes one by one to the shaved areas of the muscles using double-sided tape.
Ask the subject to perform a plantarflexing/dorsiflexing contraction against resistance after placing each electrode.
Examine the waveforms on an oscilloscope to ensure that the EMG signal has a high SNR.
If the signal SNR is poor, move the electrodes until a location with a high SNR is found.
Make sure that the subject’s movements are not hindered by the EMG cables.
Attach a reflective marker to the shank with a strap for shank angle measurement.
Place the shank marker as high as possible on the shank.
Have the subject put on the body harness.
Attach a reflect marker to the subject’s waist with a strap for upper body angle measurement.
Ensure that the waist reflective marker is placed at the mid-point between the left and right PSISs.
Ensure that the subject’s clothing does not cover the waist reflective surface.
Have the subject get on the standing apparatus.
Adjust the subject’s foot position to align the lateral and medial malleoli of each leg with the pedal’s axis of rotation.
Outline the subject’s foot positions with a marker.
Instruct the subject to keep their feet in the same locations during the experiments.
Adjust the vertical position of the laser range finders to point to the center of the reflective markers.
Adjust the horizontal distance between the laser range finder and reflective markers for optimal mid-range operation.
Have the subject lean forward and backward about the ankle.
Ensure that the lasers remain within their working range.
Measure the height of the laser range finders with respect to the ankle axis of rotation.
Inform the subject of what to expect for each trial condition.
Instruct the subject to stand quietly with hands at the side while looking forward.
Instruct the subject to maintain balance during real-world perturbations.
Start data acquisition once the subject has established a stable behavior.
Provide the subject with sufficient rest period after each trial to avoid fatigue.
Communicate with the subject to see if they need more time.
Perform a 2-min test 2 h before the subject’s arrival to examine sensor data for irregularly large noises or offsets.
Resolve any identified problems in the recorded sensor data before the subject arrives.
Perform a 2-min quiet standing trial with no perturbations.
Run the perturbation and acquire data for 2−3 min for perturbed experiments.
Apply pedal perturbations if investigating the role of somatosensory system/ankle stiffness in standing.
Apply visual perturbations if examining the role of vision in postural control.
Apply visual and pedal perturbations simultaneously if examining the interaction of the two systems in postural control.
Perform a minimum of 3 trials for each specific perturbation.
Acquire visually perturbed trials for 2 min according to the steps in sections 1.1 and 1.2.
Use a trapezoidal signal (TrapZ) with a peak-to-peak amplitude of 0.087 rad and a velocity of 0.105 rad/s.
Hold the pedal position constant at the zero angle.
Decimate the raw body angle and visual perturbation signals such that the highest observable frequency is 10 Hz.
Check the data visually after each trial to ensure that the acquired signals are of high quality.
Perform mechanically perturbed trials for 2 min.
Use a pseudo-random binary sequences (PRBS) perturbation with a peak-to-peak amplitude of 0.02 rad and a switching interval of 200 ms.
Ensure that the pedal mean angle is zero.
Differentiate the foot signal once to obtain foot velocity.
Differentiate the foot signal twice to obtain foot acceleration.
Differentiate the foot signal three times to obtain its jerk.
Differentiate the torque to obtain its velocity and acceleration using a specified command.
Compute the location of local maxima and minima of the foot velocity to locate pulses.
Use a specific command for computing the location of local maxima and minima.
Design an 8th order Butterworth low-pass filter with a corner frequency of 50 Hz.
Filter all signals using the designed Butterworth filter with zero-phase shift.
Plot the foot velocity to visually estimate the time period between extrema and start of the pulse.
Identify the point where the foot velocity is zero before reaching peak velocity, occurring 25 ms prior to the velocity extrema.
Compute the ankle background torque as the mean of the ankle torque 25 ms prior to the start of each pulse.
Find the minimum and maximum of all the background torques for all pulses.
Extract the torque data of 65 ms after the pulse start as the intrinsic torque segment.
Compute the change in the kth intrinsic torque segment from its initial value.
Find the intrinsic stiffness parameters for each group using the backslash (\) operator.
Extract the fourth element as the low frequency intrinsic stiffness.
Estimate the corresponding low frequency intrinsic stiffness for all groups (bins).
Divide all estimated low frequency stiffness values by the subject’s critical stiffness.
Convert the ankle background torque to ankle background COP position by dividing the ankle background torques with the corresponding measured vertical forces.
Plot the converted COP positions as a function of center of pressure.
